content: Regulatory Framework and Compliance Monitoring Key Amendments to the Mine Health and Safety Act The regulatory framework governing the South African mining sector is fundamentally anchored by the Mine Health and Safety Act (MHSA), a critical piece of legislation designed to regulate safety standards, protect workers from occupational hazards, and continuously improve overall safety measures within the industry. These legislative adjustments reflect a concerted effort by regulatory authorities to respond to historical vulnerabilities in mining operations and to enforce stricter compliance monitoring mechanisms across the sector. A primary focus of the regulatory discourse during this period has been the enhancement of legal obligations placed upon mining employers. Furthermore, regulatory authorities targeted the ambiguities inherent in previous statutory language, particularly concerning the training and preparation of mineworkers. Discussions surrounding the amendment of training standards emphasized the removal of the qualifying phrase "as far as reasonably practicable" from employer obligations [31] . By eliminating this caveat, the proposed amendments aimed to impose absolute, strict legal requirements on employers to ensure comprehensive and proper training, thereby removing loopholes that could previously be exploited to justify inadequate safety preparations [31] . These regulatory updates specifically revised the permissible exposure limits (PELs) and time-weighted averages (TWAs) for highly hazardous particulates, most notably respirable dust and crystalline silica [30] . The tightening of these exposure parameters was viewed as a critical step toward ensuring a healthier working environment, directly addressing the historical prevalence of occupational lung diseases such as silicosis within the South African mining workforce [30] . The intersection of occupational safety and broader environmental legislation has also begun to shape the compliance landscape. The promulgation of the Climate Change Act 22 of 2024 introduced comprehensive decarbonization strategies that, while primarily environmentally focused, indirectly influence safety compliance frameworks within the mining sector [33] . Furthermore, legislative developments continued to evolve beyond 2024, with new directives introduced in 2025 that emphasized stringent minimum safety standards and enhanced compliance requirements for all operational mines [31] .
